data.title: The Big Snack Bowl Mix-Up: Discovering Addition
data.subject: Math
data.overview: Join two mini snack piles into one big party bowl to discover how addition works! Children practice one-to-one counting with real objects and watch numbers grow as two separate groups combine into a total sum.
learningObjectives: Accurately count up to 5 individual objects in two separate sets using one-to-one correspondence.
Demonstrate that combining two distinct groups produces a larger total quantity (the sum).
Express the addition relationship verbally using terms such as 'and', 'put together', and 'makes'.

materials.item: Small cups or mini paper plates

steps.title: Set Up Your Tasting Stations
steps.instruction: Place your two small cups side by side on the table. Place the larger bowl directly behind them to make a celebration station!
steps.tip: Using two different colored cups helps keep the two starting groups clear in your mind.

steps.title: Count the First Snack Group
steps.instruction: Pick one type of snack. Touch each piece with your finger as you count aloud: '1, 2, 3.' Drop those 3 pieces into the first small cup.

checkpoint.question: How many items did you drop into cup number one?

steps.scienceNote: Touching each item as you say each number is called one-to-one correspondence. It anchors the number name to a physical amount.

steps.title: Count the Second Snack Group
steps.instruction: Pick your second snack type. Count out 2 pieces one by one: '1, 2.' Place these 2 pieces into the second small cup.

checkpoint.question: Do both cups have snacks inside them right now?

steps.tip: Keep the snacks inside their cups for now so we can see two distinct sets.

steps.title: Pour and Combine!
steps.instruction: Take cup number one and pour all 3 pieces into the big bowl. Next, take cup number two and pour all 2 pieces right in with them!
steps.tip: Say out loud: 'Three snacks and two snacks are coming together!'

steps.title: Count the Grand Total
steps.instruction: Line up all the snacks from the big bowl in a straight row across your table. Touch each one and count the new combined group from left to right.

checkpoint.question: What is the total number of snacks in your row now?

steps.scienceNote: When we push two groups together, we are doing addition! The new, larger number is called the sum.

steps.title: Tell the Math Story
steps.instruction: Say your math sentence out loud to your helper: '3 snacks plus 2 snacks makes 5 snacks!' Optional: Draw 3 dots and 2 dots on your paper to match.

checkpoint.question: Is the number of snacks in the big bowl bigger than what was in just one cup?

reflectionPrompts.question: What happened to the number of snacks when we poured both cups into the big bowl?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Demonstrate that combining two distinct groups produces a larger total quantity (the sum).
reflectionPrompts.hint: Think about whether you have more snacks or fewer snacks in the big bowl than in just one little cup.

reflectionPrompts.question: If you started with 4 pretzels in one cup and 1 pretzel in the other, how could you find out how many there are all together?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Express the addition relationship verbally using terms such as 'and', 'put together', and 'makes'.
reflectionPrompts.hint: What step did we do with our cups and the big bowl to count them all?

reflectionPrompts.question: Where do you see people putting things together to make a bigger group in your house?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Express the addition relationship verbally using terms such as 'and', 'put together', and 'makes'.
reflectionPrompts.hint: Think about putting toys into a toy box, adding laundry to a basket, or setting forks on the dinner table.

documentationPrompt.instruction: Take a photo of your lined-up snacks next to the big bowl, or take a picture of your paper with your dots drawn on it.
documentationPrompt.suggestedCaption: We made snack math! [Child's Name] combined ___ [snack 1] and ___ [snack 2] to get a grand total of ___ snacks!

extensions.title: The Mystery Bowl (Adding Zero)
extensions.description: Put 4 snacks into the first cup and leave the second cup completely empty (0 snacks). Pour them both into the bowl and count the total. Discuss what happens when you add zero!

extensions.title: Three-Cup Mountain Mix
extensions.description: Add a third small cup! Put 1 snack in Cup A, 2 in Cup B, and 2 in Cup C. Pour all three into the big bowl and count up to find the new sum.

safetyNotes: Adult helper recommended to assist with counting and food handling.
Be mindful of potential food allergies when selecting edible counters (nuts, dairy, gluten).
Ensure non-food counters (such as buttons or beads) are large enough to avoid choking hazards.

problems.question: What is two apples and three more apples in all?
problems.rationale: When you put a group of two apples together with three more apples, you can count them all together: one, two, three, four, five. Combining two and three gives a total of five apples.
problems.teachingNote: Encourage young learners to use fingers or physical counters to model the two separate groups before joining them together to count the total.
successCriteria: Combine two distinct groups of physical objects to find the total amount up to 5.
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.question: What does the plus sign mean?
problems.rationale: The plus sign means to join or put groups together to find out how many in all. When we see the plus sign between numbers, we combine them into a bigger total. Taking away is subtraction, which uses the minus sign instead.
problems.teachingNote: Have students practice making the plus sign with their index fingers while saying 'put together' to build a strong physical and verbal association.
successCriteria: Identify the plus sign in an addition sentence
Explain that the plus sign means to put together or join amounts
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.statement: When you put 2 toys and 1 toy together, you get a bigger number than 2.
problems.rationale: When we combine groups of items through addition, the total amount increases because we are putting things together. Adding 1 toy to 2 toys gives us 3 toys, and 3 is a bigger number than 2.
problems.teachingNote: Reinforce that addition always results in a larger total quantity when combining positive numbers, helping students overcome the misconception that putting things together might leave the amount unchanged.
successCriteria: Explain how putting things together makes a bigger number
Understand that combining sets increases the total quantity
